articles.title: What Not to Automate: Five Replies That Should Stay Human
articles.excerpt: Auto-replies earn their keep on the repetitive share of a support inbox: prices, stock, shipping times, order status, opening hours. The mistake is letting the same system answer everything. Some repl…
articles.body: Auto-replies earn their keep on the repetitive share of a support inbox: prices, stock, shipping times, order status, opening hours. The mistake is letting the same system answer everything. Some replies carry asymmetric cost — a wrong answer about courier hours is fixable; a wrong answer that touches money, safety, or someone's temper is not. The test worth applying is reversibility: automate the conversations where a wrong reply costs little, and keep a person on the five kinds below, where it does not. Disputes and Money: Escalations, Then Price Fights One: dispute escalations. Once a customer names a dispute — "I'll open a case," "this is the third time," any mention of the platform, a chargeback, or consumer rights — the conversation is no longer about the parcel.

articles.body: Short answer: choose managed cloud object storage for the easiest Node.js avatar upload path, unless tenant isolation requires a storage plane your team must operate itself. Managed cloud object storage is the easiest path for Node.js avatar uploads, but I would choose self-hosted storage when the tenant boundary is the primary control rather than an implementation detail. The deciding question is not how quickly an HTTP multipart request can become an image; it is whether a healthtech platform can prove that an avatar, a training artifact, and a deletion request stay inside the right tenant boundary for their entire lifecycle.

articles.title: Measuring First-Response Time Without Punishing the Wrong Shift
articles.excerpt: First-response time is the metric every support team tracks and the one most often measured unfairly. A flat weekly average blends a holiday-weekend backlog with a calm Tuesday morning and says almost…
articles.body: First-response time is the metric every support team tracks and the one most often measured unfairly. A flat weekly average blends a holiday-weekend backlog with a calm Tuesday morning and says almost nothing. Worse, it can punish the shift that inherited the queue instead of the process that built it. Fairness here is not a nicety: an unfair number gets gamed, and a gamed number hides the actual problem. Fix the Starting Point First The same inbox supports three clocks. Clock A starts when the customer sends the first message. Clock B starts when the message is assigned to an agent or queue. Clock C starts when an agent actually opens it. If the report does not say which clock it uses, the number is decorative. For staffing decisions use Clock A — it represents the customer's wait.

articles.title: Analog astronauts: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.excerpt: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.body: I have been dreaming of doing research in space as an astronaut my whole life, but for some reason, the thought of working underwater made me nervous. I’ve known for a long time that astronauts train underwater to simulate different scenarios they’re likely to experience in space. Diving was never an issue for me, either — I even made it as far as becoming a certified rescue diver. So what was the problem? This summer, I led a simulated space mission in an underwater habitat called the Jules’ Undersea Lab. It is a research station that is located 22 feet (6.7 meters) underwater near Key Largo, Florida. You have to scuba dive to get in and out of the station. To become an aquanaut , you have to stay underwater for at least 24 hours in a so-called state of saturation.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 26, 2004: Cassini spacecraft takes 1st-ever closeup photos of Saturn moon Titan
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. The Cassini spacecraft would later drop off a probe on Titan named Huygens, which was a European spacecraft that hitched a ride to the Saturn system with the Cassini mission. But before Cassini dropped off its robotic passenger, it flew by Titan a few times and took some amazing photos . Cassini completed its first flyby on July 3, 2004, but when it swung by a second time on Oct. 26, it got about 300 times closer than it did the first time. At the closest point of this flyby, Cassini was 745 miles (1,200 kilometers) away from the surface of Titan. The spacecraft took hundreds of photos during this flyby , and these were the highest resolution views of Titan anyone had ever seen.

articles.title: NASA ends Swift space telescope mission after failed rescue attempt
articles.excerpt: NASA has officially ended the mission of its Swift Observatory, after a private satellite failed to meet up with the aging spacecraft in orbit.
articles.body: NASA has officially ended the mission of its Swift space telescope, after a private satellite failed in its bold bid to rescue the aging spacecraft. That rescue mission was led by the Arizona company Katalyst Space Technologies, whose LINK spacecraft tried to meet up with Swift this summer to boost its orbit. That didn't work out, however, so Swift continues its fall back toward Earth. The telescope is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere "in the next few weeks," NASA said in a statement on Friday (Oct. 23). That statement served primarily to announce the end of the Swift mission after more than 20 very productive years. The telescope launched to Earth orbit in November 2004, tasked with studying gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) — the most powerful explosions in the cosmos.
